questions.title: Why acetylcholine is unsuitable clinically
questions.question: Acetylcholine is not used in clinical practice because:

options.C: The doses required are very high

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acetylcholine's clinical unsuitability is not primarily about toxicity -- it is about the impractical dosing its non-selectivity and instant hydrolysis would require.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cost is not the reason acetylcholine is avoided clinically -- more selective, longer-acting cholinomimetics such as carbachol or bethanechol are chosen instead for pharmacological, not economic, reasons.
explanations.C: Correct. Acetylcholine acts non-selectively on both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors and is hydrolysed almost instantly by acetylcholinesterase and plasma cholinesterase. Together these mean the doses needed to sustain any therapeutic effect would be impractically high. This is why more selective, AChE-resistant agents are used instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rapid hydrolysis is real, but the printed institutional answer names the resulting dosing impracticality as the reason acetylcholine is unsuitable, not the hydrolysis fact by itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that acetylcholine is unsuitable for clinical use because the doses required would be impractically high.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: The doses required are very high"

questions.title: Muscarinic stimulation causes spasm of accommodation
questions.question: Which of the following is the effect of stimulating muscarinic receptors?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Muscarinic stimulation of vascular endothelium releases nitric oxide, producing vasodilation, not vasoconstriction.
explanations.B: Correct. Muscarinic stimulation contracts the ciliary muscle in the eye. This sustained contraction fixes the lens in its near-vision focus, a state called spasm of accommodation. It is one of the classic ocular effects of a muscarinic agonist.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Muscarinic stimulation causes miosis (pupillary constriction) via sphincter pupillae contraction, not mydriasis, which is instead an antimuscarinic effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Muscarinic stimulation increases, not decreases, glandular secretion, so it produces the opposite of xerostomia -- xerostomia is an antimuscarinic effect.

questions.learning_objective: State that muscarinic stimulation causes spasm of accommodation, not mydriasis.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Spasm of accommodation"

questions.title: Bethanechol for post-op ileus
questions.question: Following gastrointestinal surgery, your patient remains severely constipated. Bowel sounds are absent. The drug you are most likely to prescribe to treat this problem is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acetylcholine's impractically rapid hydrolysis and non-selectivity make it unsuitable for a sustained clinical effect like restoring bowel motility.
explanations.B: Correct. Bethanechol is a direct-acting muscarinic agonist that resists acetylcholinesterase and is selective for GI and urinary smooth muscle. This combination makes it the drug of choice for restoring bowel motility in postoperative (non-obstructive) ileus. Absent bowel sounds and severe constipation after abdominal surgery is exactly this indication.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Atropine is an antimuscarinic and would further reduce, not restore, GI motility -- the opposite of what this patient needs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pilocarpine's established indications are ocular (glaucoma) and glandular (xerostomia), not GI motility -- bethanechol is the muscarinic agonist selective for that indication instead.

questions.learning_objective: State that bethanechol treats postoperative bowel atony/ileus.

questions.title: Carbachol overdose but not neostigmine overdose causes hypotension
questions.question: An overdose of muscarinic agonist carbachol but not an overdose of acetylcholinesterase inhibitor neostigmine could cause the following:

explanations.A: Correct. Carbachol, a direct-acting agonist, can act at muscarinic receptors with no cholinergic innervation, such as vascular endothelium. Stimulating these non-innervated receptors can produce pronounced hypotension. Neostigmine, an indirect-acting agent, can only potentiate acetylcholine where it is already being released, so it cannot reach this non-innervated site the same way.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both a direct-acting muscarinic agonist and an indirect-acting AChE inhibitor can produce bronchoconstriction, since both raise muscarinic tone at the (innervated) airway smooth muscle -- this is not the distinguishing effect asked for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cholinergic crisis is the distinguishing overdose effect of the indirect-acting agent (neostigmine), from its potentiation of nicotinic transmission at the neuromuscular junction -- not of the direct-acting agent, so this is backwards from what the question asks.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both agents would be expected to cause miosis, since both raise muscarinic tone at the (innervated) eye -- this is not the distinguishing effect.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Both agents would be expected to cause sweating, since sweat glands are innervated cholinergic sympathetic effectors reached by either drug -- this is not the distinguishing effect.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish a direct-acting agonist's overdose effect at non-innervated receptors (hypotension) from an indirect-acting inhibitor's overdose effect.

questions.title: Carbachol does not cause mydriasis (I)
questions.question: Characteristics of carbachol include all of the following Except:

options.A: It causes a decrease in intraocular pressure.
options.B: It exerts both nicotinic and muscarinic effects.

explanations.A: This IS a characteristic of carbachol, so it is not the exception. Its miotic action opens the trabecular drainage angle, decreasing intraocular pressure.
explanations.B: This IS a characteristic of carbachol, so it is not the exception. Unlike acetylcholine or pilocarpine, it exerts dual nicotinic and muscarinic activity.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is NOT a characteristic of carbachol. As a muscarinic agonist, carbachol causes miosis, pupillary constriction, not mydriasis. Mydriasis is instead an antimuscarinic effect, the pharmacological opposite.
explanations.D: This IS a characteristic of carbachol, so it is not the exception. It is a parasympathetic (cholinomimetic) agent, acting to mimic parasympathetic stimulation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify mydriasis as NOT a characteristic of carbachol.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: It causes mydriasis."

questions.title: Carbachol does not cause mydriasis (II)
questions.question: Characteristics of carbachol include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.D: It exerts both nicotinic and muscarinic effects

explanations.A: This IS a characteristic of carbachol, so it is not the exception. Its resistance to acetylcholinesterase hydrolysis gives it a longer duration of action than acetylcholine.
explanations.B: This IS a characteristic of carbachol, so it is not the exception. Its miotic action lowers intraocular pressure, the basis of its ophthalmic use.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is NOT a characteristic of carbachol. As a muscarinic agonist, carbachol causes miosis, the opposite of mydriasis. Mydriasis is instead an antimuscarinic effect.
explanations.D: This IS a characteristic of carbachol, so it is not the exception. Its dual nicotinic and muscarinic activity distinguishes it from a muscarinic-selective agonist like pilocarpine.

questions.learning_objective: Identify mydriasis as NOT a characteristic of carbachol.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: It causes mydriasis"

questions.title: Bronchi dilation is NOT a muscarinic effect
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a primary effect of stimulating muscarinic receptors?

explanations.A: This IS a primary muscarinic effect, so it is not the answer. Muscarinic stimulation of the sphincter pupillae causes miosis.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is NOT a primary muscarinic effect. M3 muscarinic receptors on bronchiolar smooth muscle are Gq-coupled and raise IP3/DAG. This produces bronchoconstriction, the opposite of bronchi dilation.
explanations.C: This IS a primary muscarinic effect, so it is not the answer. Ciliary muscle contraction from muscarinic stimulation produces spasm of accommodation.
explanations.D: This IS a primary muscarinic effect, so it is not the answer. Muscarinic stimulation of vascular endothelium releases nitric oxide, producing vasodilation.

questions.subtopic: Muscarinic receptor subtypes and signal transduction
questions.learning_objective: Identify bronchodilation as NOT a muscarinic effect (muscarinic stimulation instead causes bronchoconstriction).

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Bronchi dilation"

questions.hold: Printed key names Physostigmine as the direct-acting cholinomimetic among {Carbachol, Physostigmine, Isoflurophate, Edrophonium}, but physostigmine is pharmacologically an indirect-acting agent (a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor), same as isoflurophate (irreversible AChE inhibitor) and edrophonium (very short-acting AChE inhibitor) -- all three of the printed distractors are indirect-acting. Carbachol (option A) is the only genuinely direct-acting receptor agonist among the four options and is the pharmacologically correct answer. Held per the printed-key-vs-pharmacology-fact conflict rule (same handling as Q19, Q25, Q47 in this lane's earlier clusters), not resolved by inference.

questions.title: Bethanechol for urinary retention
questions.question: What is bethanechol most commonly used for?

explanations.A: Correct. Bethanechol is a direct-acting, acetylcholinesterase-resistant muscarinic agonist selective for GI and urinary smooth muscle. Stimulating detrusor contraction restores bladder emptying. This makes it the standard drug for non-obstructive urinary retention, alongside its use for postoperative bowel atony.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lowering blood pressure via vasodilation is not bethanechol's characteristic indication -- its selective action targets GI and urinary smooth muscle, not the vasculature.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Decreasing intraocular pressure is pilocarpine's characteristic ocular indication, not bethanechol's -- bethanechol is instead selective for GI/urinary smooth muscle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bethanechol has minimal cardiovascular activity by design, which is precisely what makes it safe for GI/urinary indications without producing significant bradycardia.

questions.learning_objective: State that bethanechol's most common use is treating urinary retention.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: For urinary retention"

questions.title: Catarrhal inflammation: excess mucosal secretion
questions.question: The main feature of catarrhal inflammation is:

options.B: Excess secretions from superficial mucosal surface

explanations.A: Incorrect. A granulomatous reaction describes a distinct pattern of chronic inflammation, not the acute catarrhal pattern.
explanations.B: Correct. Catarrhal inflammation is a pattern of acute non-suppurative inflammation whose main feature is excess mucous or serous secretion from a superficial mucosal surface. This distinguishes it from the pus-forming pattern of suppurative inflammation. It also distinguishes it from deep ulceration or abscess formation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Abscess formation is a localized pattern of suppurative inflammation, an entirely different mechanism from catarrhal inflammation's excess secretion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cellulitis is the diffuse pattern of suppurative inflammation, not the excess-secretion pattern that defines catarrhal inflammation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Deep ulceration implies substantial tissue destruction, which catarrhal inflammation, confined to the superficial mucosal epithelium, does not produce.

questions.learning_objective: State that catarrhal inflammation's main feature is excess mucosal secretion.
questions.module_subject: AUN-MPT-104 > Pathology > Acute non suppurative inflammation

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Excess secretions from superficial mucosal surface"

questions.title: Catarrhal inflammation resolves with tissue repair
questions.question: The usual outcome of acute catarrhal inflammation:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Suppuration describes a distinct, pus-forming pattern of inflammation, not the usual outcome of catarrhal inflammation's superficial mucosal irritation.
explanations.B: Correct. Because catarrhal inflammation involves only the superficial mucosal epithelium without substantial tissue destruction, its usual outcome is complete resolution with tissue repair. This is unlike more destructive inflammatory patterns. Once the irritant clears, the epithelium repairs itself fully.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ulceration and perforation imply substantial tissue destruction, which the superficial, non-destructive catarrhal pattern does not typically produce.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fibrosis and deformation are outcomes of more destructive or chronic inflammatory processes, not the usual outcome of catarrhal inflammation, which resolves completely instead.

questions.learning_objective: State that catarrhal inflammation's usual outcome is resolution and tissue repair.
questions.module_subject: AUN-MPT-104 > Pathology > Acute non suppurative inflammation

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Resolution and tissue repair"

questions.title: Neostigmine differs from pilocarpine at skeletal muscle
questions.question: Neostigmine differs from pilocarpine in having effects on

explanations.A: Incorrect. Both a muscarinic agonist like pilocarpine and an indirect-acting agent like neostigmine can affect muscarinic (innervated) bladder tone -- this is not the distinguishing site.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both agents can affect heart rate via muscarinic M2 receptors at the (innervated) heart -- this is not the distinguishing site.
explanations.C: Correct. Neostigmine's indirect action lets endogenous acetylcholine accumulate wherever it is already being released, including the skeletal neuromuscular junction's nicotinic receptors. Pilocarpine, a muscarinic-selective direct agonist, does not significantly affect this nicotinic site. Skeletal muscle is therefore the site where neostigmine has an effect that pilocarpine does not.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both agents can affect muscarinic (innervated) bowel motility -- this is not the distinguishing site.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Both agents can affect muscarinic (innervated) salivary gland secretion -- this is not the distinguishing site.

questions.learning_objective: State that neostigmine, unlike pilocarpine, affects skeletal muscle via nicotinic NMJ potentiation.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: skeletal muscle"

questions.title: Neostigmine overdose but not carbachol overdose causes cholinergic crisis
questions.question: An overdose of acetylcholinesterase inhibitor neostigmine but not an overdose of muscarinic agonist carbachol could cause the following:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Both agents raise muscarinic tone at the (innervated) eye and would be expected to cause miosis -- this is not the distinguishing effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both agents raise muscarinic tone at innervated sweat glands and would be expected to cause sweating -- this is not the distinguishing effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is carbachol's overdose, not neostigmine's, that can produce hypotension, from direct action at non-innervated vascular muscarinic receptors -- this option is backwards from what the question asks.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both agents raise muscarinic tone at (innervated) airway smooth muscle and would be expected to cause bronchoconstriction -- this is not the distinguishing effect.
explanations.E: Correct. Neostigmine's indirect action potentiates acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction's nicotinic receptors, unlike carbachol's muscarinic-selective action. Overdosing neostigmine produces excess nicotinic stimulation at the neuromuscular junction, causing muscle weakness and potential paralysis. This nicotinic-overstimulation picture, a cholinergic crisis, is what carbachol overdose does not produce.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish an indirect-acting inhibitor's overdose effect at the neuromuscular junction (cholinergic crisis) from a direct-acting agonist's overdose effect.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Cholinergic crisis"

questions.title: Edrophonium distinguishes myasthenic from cholinergic crisis
questions.question: Which of the following is the best drug for distinguishing between myasthenic crisis (insufficient therapy) and cholinergic crisis (excessive therapy)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Physostigmine's longer-acting inhibition is used for maintenance therapy, not diagnosis -- it lacks the brief action that makes edrophonium safe for a repeatable diagnostic test.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase in organophosphate poisoning -- an unrelated indication, not a diagnostic test for myasthenic vs cholinergic crisis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects generally but does not distinguish the two crises, which differ in their nicotinic (neuromuscular) response to a brief anticholinesterase test dose.
explanations.D: Correct. Edrophonium's very brief, fast-onset acetylcholinesterase inhibition makes it ideal diagnostically. A test dose transiently improves strength if the cause is myasthenic crisis (undertreatment) but worsens weakness if the cause is cholinergic crisis (overtreatment). Because its effect wears off within minutes, the test is safe and repeatable.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Donepezil is a long-acting anticholinesterase used for Alzheimer's disease maintenance therapy, not a short-acting diagnostic agent for this crisis distinction.

questions.learning_objective: State that edrophonium's brief action makes it the diagnostic test for myasthenic vs cholinergic crisis.

questions.title: Echothiophate is irreversible
questions.question: Which of the following drugs is irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neostigmine forms a temporary carbamate-enzyme complex and its inhibition wanes over time -- it is reversible, not irreversible.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pilocarpine is not a cholinesterase inhibitor at all -- it is a direct-acting muscarinic receptor agonist, a different mechanism entirely.
explanations.C: Correct. Echothiophate is an organophosphate-type acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that phosphorylates the enzyme's active site essentially irreversibly. Despite this systemic organophosphate-like toxicity potential, it is used topically for glaucoma. Its long-duration miotic effect there lowers intraocular pressure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Physostigmine, like neostigmine, forms a temporary carbamate-enzyme complex and is reversible, not irreversible.

questions.learning_objective: Identify echothiophate as the irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor.

questions.title: Farm child with muscarinic-excess symptoms: insecticide exposure
questions.question: A 5-year-old child becomes ill while visiting relatives who have a farm in Arkansas. His symptoms include severe abdominal cramps with vomiting and diarrhea and profuse lacrimation and salivation. Pupillary constriction is marked. The most likely cause is exposure to

explanations.A: Incorrect. Common rat poisons (anticoagulant rodenticides) cause bleeding, not this cholinergic-excess picture of cramps, diarrhoea, lacrimation, salivation and miosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) poisoning causes metabolic acidosis and renal injury, not this muscarinic-excess symptom pattern.
explanations.C: Correct. Organophosphate insecticides irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, letting acetylcholine accumulate at muscarinic receptors throughout the body. The resulting muscarinic-excess picture is exactly what is described: GI cramps with vomiting and diarrhoea, profuse lacrimation and salivation, and miosis. A farm setting is a classic exposure context for this poisoning.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Herbicide exposure does not typically produce this specific muscarinic-excess (cholinergic) symptom cluster.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lead-based paint exposure causes a different, typically chronic and neurocognitive/GI toxidrome, not this acute muscarinic-excess picture.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the muscarinic-excess symptom picture as organophosphate insecticide poisoning.

questions.title: Elderly farm suicide attempt: organophosphate pesticide
questions.question: An elderly female who lives in a farm house was brought to the emergency room in serious condition after ingesting a liquid from an unlabeled bottle found near her bed, apparently in a suicide attempt. She presented with diarrhea, frequent urination, convulsions, breathing difficulties, constricted pupils (miosis), and excessive salivation. Which of the following is correct regarding this patient?

options.A: The symptoms are consistent with sympathetic activation.
options.B: Her symptoms can be treated using a cholinergic agonist.
options.C: Her symptoms can be treated using an anticholinesterase agent.
options.D: She most likely consumed an organophosphate pesticide.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Diarrhoea, frequent urination, miosis and salivation are a muscarinic-excess (parasympathetic-excess) picture, not a sympathetic one -- sympathetic activation would instead produce mydriasis, dry mouth and constipation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Giving a cholinergic agonist would add to, not treat, an already cholinergic-excess poisoning -- the treatment instead uses an antimuscarinic (atropine) plus an enzyme reactivator (pralidoxime).
explanations.C: Incorrect. An anticholinesterase would further raise acetylcholine, worsening rather than treating a poisoning that is already caused by excess acetylcholine from cholinesterase inhibition.
explanations.D: Correct. The muscarinic-excess picture -- diarrhoea, urination, convulsions, breathing difficulty, miosis, salivation -- is the classic presentation of organophosphate poisoning. A farm setting and unlabeled bottle are a typical exposure context. This poisoning irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, flooding muscarinic receptors with acetylcholine.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the muscarinic-excess symptom picture as organophosphate pesticide poisoning, and rule out cholinergic treatments.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: She most likely consumed an organophosphate pesticide."

questions.title: Sarin exposure causes miosis
questions.question: Sarin is a volatile nerve agent that inhibits cholinesterase enzymes. Which of the following symptoms would you expect to see in a patient exposed to sarin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sarin's muscarinic excess produces bradycardia via M2 receptors on the heart, not tachycardia -- tachycardia is instead seen after atropine treatment reverses the poisoning.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Muscarinic excess increases, not decreases, glandular secretion, producing profuse salivation rather than dry mouth -- dry mouth is an antimuscarinic (post-treatment) effect.
explanations.C: Correct. Sarin inhibits acetylcholinesterase, flooding muscarinic receptors with acetylcholine. Among its muscarinic-excess effects is pupillary constriction. Miosis is therefore an expected finding in sarin exposure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Muscarinic excess increases bladder detrusor contraction, producing increased urination rather than urinary retention, which is instead an antimuscarinic effect.

questions.learning_objective: State that miosis is an expected finding in nerve-agent (sarin) exposure.

questions.title: Muscarinic antagonists worsen radiation-induced xerostomia
questions.question: Head and neck irradiation in cancer patients can decrease salivary secretion and cause dry mouth. All of the following drugs or classes of drugs are theoretically useful in improving secretion of saliva in these patients except:

explanations.A: This class IS theoretically useful, so it is not the exception. Pilocarpine is a direct muscarinic agonist and established sialagogue.
explanations.B: Correct. Muscarinic antagonists block muscarinic receptors on the remaining salivary gland tissue, reducing rather than improving secretion. This is the opposite direction from what radiation-induced xerostomia needs. They are therefore the one class among the options that would worsen, not improve, dry mouth.
explanations.C: This class IS theoretically useful, so it is not the exception. Anticholinesterases raise acetylcholine at remaining glandular tissue, increasing secretion.
explanations.D: This class IS theoretically useful, so it is not the exception. Muscarinic agonists generally increase glandular secretion by direct receptor stimulation.
explanations.E: This class IS theoretically useful, so it is not the exception. Neostigmine, an anticholinesterase, raises acetylcholine and can increase salivary secretion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify muscarinic antagonists as the class that would worsen, not improve, radiation-induced xerostomia.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Muscarinic antagonists."
